lines.text: necromancer, sorcerer, a conjurer who
professes to call up the dead by means
of incantations and magic formulas, in
order that they may give response as to
doubtful or future things; comp. 1 Sam.
21, 6. 2 Chr. 33, 6. Plur. אֹבוֹת Lev. 19,
Spec. put a) For the divining spirit, the
foreboding demon, python, supposed to be
present in the body of such a conjurer;
comp. Acts 16, 16. So Lev. 20, 27 אִישׁ
אוֹ אִשָּׁה כִּי יִהְיֶה בָהֶם אוֹב a man or a
woman in whom is the spirit of divina-
tion, Eng. ‘ familiar spirit.’ 1 Sam. 28, 8
קָסֳמִי־נָא לִי בָּאוֹב divine unto me by the
foreboding spirit; whence such a sorce-
ress is called אֵשֶׁת בַּעֲלַת אוֹב a woman in
whom is a divining spirit, 1 Sam. 28, 7. 8.
b) For the dead, the shade or spirit
evoked. Is. 29,4 וְהָיָה כְּאוֹב מֵאֶרֶץ קוֹלֵךְ and
thy voice shall be like a shade out of the
ground.—The LXX usually render אֹבוֹת
by ἐγγαστρίμυθοι, ventriloquists, and
correctly; since among the ancients this
power of ventriloquism was often mis-
used for the purposes of magic.—As to
the connection between these two signifi-
cations of bottle and necromancer, it prob.
arose from regarding the conjurer, while
possessed by the demon, as a bottle, i. e.
vessel, case, in which the demon was
contained. Hence
אוֹבֹת (water-skins) Oboth, pr. n. of a
station of the Israelites in the desert,
Num. 21, 10. 34, 43. It must be sought
in the desert on the eastern skirts of
Idumea, not far from Moab.
אוֹבִיל 1 Chr. 27, 30, Obil, pr. n. of an
Ishmaelite. who had charge of the cam-
els of David. It signifies pr. chief of the
camels, like Arab. أَبَّالٌ and أَبِيلٌ from
إِبْلٌ camel.—The form אוֹבִיל is for אוֹבֵל,
as תּוֹמִיךְ for תּוֹמֵךְ Ps. 16, 5.
אוּבָל and אֻבָל, m. (r. יָבַל) a stream,
river, only in Dan. 8, 2. 3. 6.
* אוּד and אִיד obsol. root. 1. to bend,
to inflect, Arab. آدَ mid. Waw; then to
turn, to turn about or over, to stir, see
subst. אוּד, אוֹדוֹת; also to put around,
to surround, see אֵד. Corresponding is
Heb. עוּד. Hence
2. to load, to burden, to press down with
weight; whence آبِل heavy, burden-
some, أَوْدَةٌ a load, weight, مَآوِدُ mis-
fortunes, evils, calamities, by which one
is weighed down; see אֵיד.
3. i. q. أَدَّ for أَيَدَ, to be strong, ro-
bust; Conj. II, to strengthen, to aid, أَيَّدَ
and آدٌّ strength, might, force; whence
Heb. מְאֹד. Comp. קָשָׁה and other verbs
which also connect the notions of weight
and strength.
אוּד m. pr. a wooden poker, with which
a fire is stirred, see r. אוּד no 1; hence
any burnt wood, a fire-brand, Zech. 3, 2.
Am. 4, 11. Is. 7, 4. Syr. and Chald. id.
Others make it i. q. عود wood.
אוֹדוֹת plur. pr. turnings, turns, see r.
אוּד no. 1; then circumstances, reasons,
causes of things. Comp. سَبَبٌ cause,
from r. סָבַב to turn about; حَالٌ way,
manner, cause, from حَالَ, חוּל, to turn
oneself; Germ. um for wegen; בִּגְלַל be-
cause of, from גָּלַל.—Found only in the
formula עַל־אוֹדוֹת i. q. עַל דְּבַר, עַל דִּבְרֵי,
for the causes, i. e. on account of, be-
cause of, propter, Gen. 21, 11. 25. 26, 32.
Ex. 18, 8; c. suff. עַל אֹדוֹתַי on my ac-
count, Josh. 14, 6. עַל כָּל־אֹדוֹת אֲשֶׁר
for all these causes that, for this very
cause that, Jer. 3, 8.—In some editt. is
found 2 Sam. 13, 16 אֶל אֹדוֹת, which
has arisen from combining two readings,
אֶל־אוֹדוֹת and עַל אוֹדוֹת.
* I. אָוָה not used in Kal, pr. to bend,
to inflect; comp. kindr. עָוָה. Hence
1. to turn aside, to take lodging, to
lodge, to dwell; i.q. Arab. أَوَى Conj. I,
II; مَأْوًى a lodging, dwelling. See
deriv. אִי.
2. i. q. Arab. أَوَى to incline, to have a
bent, i. e. to desire, to long for, to wish;
see Pi. Hithpa. and comp. חָפֵץ. Kindr.
roots are אָבָה, Lat. aveo, Arab. هَوِىَ,
Sanscr. aw, to desire.

line_status.note: The only difference is the gap after the opening quote: the print shows a clear space between ‘ and “familiar” (old-style quote spacing), as in B; everything else (italic “tion,”, “Eng.”, “28, 8” with a space after the comma) is identical in both readings and matches the print.

The Hebrew is identical in both readings and matches the print (וְהָיָה כְּאוֹב מֵאֶרֶץ קוֹלֵךְ, dagesh in kaf, plene אוֹב and קוֹל). The only difference is the reference: the print has "29,4" with no space after the comma, as in Reading B.
A narrow vertical stroke (vav) is printed between aleph and bet, carrying the first holem; the second holem sits over the bet. So the headword is plene אוֹבֹת, not defective אֹבֹת.

The mark after "Ishmaelite" is a plain baseline dot with no descending tail, unlike the clearly tailed commas after "Idumea," "27," "30," and "Obil," on the adjacent lines — so a full stop is what is printed (likely a worn or mis-set comma, but the impression is a period). Everything else is identical in both readings.

First word: the alif carries a hamza + fatha (not a madda), and the bā clearly bears a shadda + fatha, so A's أَبَّالٌ is right and B's آبَالٌ is wrong. Second word: hamza is printed above the alif (no hamza-below, unlike إِبْلٌ on line 2), and the bā has only a kasra with no shadda, so B's أَبِيلٌ is right and A's إِبِّيلٌ is wrong. Each reading is correct on one word only.
Final word is printed plene אוֹבֵל with a vav bearing holem between alef and bet, not defective אֹבֵל as in Reading B.

The second Hebrew word is printed plene: a vav with holem is visible between the tav and mem (four letters ת־ו־מ־ך, with tsere under mem and sheva under final kaph), so תּוֹמֵךְ (Reading A), not defective תֹּמֵךְ.
Second word is printed plene אוֹדוֹת: a vav with holem is visible between aleph and dalet (two holem dots over two vavs), not אֹדוֹת with holem on the aleph alone.

The Arabic word's final letter has a tall ascender with a hooked bowl (lām, not dāl), and the middle letter carries a single dot below with kasra (bā, not yā); there is also a space before the semicolon. A small superscript mark (sukūn/shadda-like) sits over the middle letter that neither reading records.
Both Arabic words carry a final nominative mark: a dammatan (printed as the "G"-like curl) above the ة of أَوْدَةٌ, and a damma above the final د of مَآوِدُ. Reading A omits both.

Second Arabic word ends in dal (no ascender), so B's أَيَلَ is wrong; but the first word's final letter carries a shadda with fatha (دَّ), so A's آدَ (madda, no shadda) is also wrong — printed is أَدَّ for أَيَدَ (geminate for hollow/weak root).

The final Arabic letter is dāl (د), as in أَيَدَ on the line above (root ʾ-y-d, Conj. II ayyada), not lām as in B; but the print also carries a fatḥa over the final dāl (the cluster of marks above reads fatḥa‑shadda on yā plus fatḥa on dāl), which A omits. The print also has a visible space before the semicolon ("bust ;").

The Arabic glyph is a dāl (open bowl with foot, no dot), not a nūn, and it carries two marks stacked above it—shadda plus tanwīn ḍamm—so آدٌّ (B) is correct; A's آنٌ misreads the letter and drops the shadda.

Under the aleph of אל the print shows three dots in a triangle (segol), not a single horizontal stroke (patach); so אֶל as in Reading A. אֹדוֹת is plene with holem on aleph and vav-holem, as both readings have.

Printed left-to-right order is אֶל־אוֹדוֹת (with maqqef) first, then "and", then עַל אוֹדוֹת at the right before the full stop; Reading A reverses the two items. Vowel points (segol, patah, two holems each) match both readings.
The final letter of the Arabic word is printed dotless (ى, alif-maqṣūra form) with fatḥa above; no two dots beneath, so Reading B's ي is wrong. Rest of line identical in both.
